title: The King and the Humble Deliverance

keywords: the angel of death and the king of the children of israel
full_text:
In ancient Jerusalem reigned a pious king who was renowned for his care of orphans, his fair administration of the courts, and his devotion to the welfare of his people. One evening, as he knelt in his private sanctuary, a radiant figure appeared before him, holding an hourglass whose sands were nearly spent.

'O King,' said the celestial visitor gently, 'your earthly work is concluded. Prepare your spirit, for with the morning light, you shall depart this life.'

The king bowed his head with humble submission, but tears fell from his eyes. The visitor asked: 'Why do you weep, O King? Do you fear the journey to your Creator?'

The king answered with sincere sorrow: 'I fear not the journey, for I trust in divine mercy. But I weep because my kingdom is threatened by a terrible drought; the granaries are half-built, the orphans are not yet provided for, and my young son lacks the maturity to govern with justice. I prayed for a few years more, not to enjoy royal banquets or wear crowns, but to complete the irrigation channels that will feed my people and to train my son in the paths of wisdom.'

Seeing the absolute purity of the king's intention, free from selfish vanity or fear of death, the celestial messenger ascended to the heavens to convey his plea.

Before the dawn tinted the sky, the visitor returned, holding the hourglass inverted, with fresh sands pouring down the glass!

'Rejoice, O King!' said the messenger. 'Your prayer has been granted because your heart sought not life for yourself, but life for the service of your people. Fifteen years are added to your reign.'

The king threw himself upon the stones in heartfelt gratitude. For the next fifteen years, he built aqueducts, established academies, and secured the peace of his realm, proving that a life dedicated to selfless service is blessed with abundance.
moral: A sincere prayer and heartfelt desire to serve others can invoke mercy and grant a renewal of purpose.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Angel of Death and the King of the Children of Israel"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
